claims.claim: Maine reference lakes held larger, older suckers than harvested lakes, where annual mortality was at least twice as high
claims.note: Article not read (the paper already flags 'abstract'). The abstract says exactly this ('Estimated annual mortality rates were at least twofold higher in harvested lakes'). The STAND-IN (Begley 2016 thesis, Chapter 1, the same 976 spawning-run fish from six lakes in 2014) supports it: harvested lakes had more than two-fold higher annual mortality than their paired reference lakes (thesis p. 17, PDF p. 31; Table 1.5, PDF p. 33); reference lakes 18.3–25.2 %/yr, harvested 35.5–67.1 %/yr, 2 to 2.8-fold (p. 27, PDF p. 41); fish older and larger in reference lakes (pp. 13–17).

claims.note: Article not read. The stand-in thesis gives a maximum observed age of 26 in one reference lake (pair B: 16 in the harvested lake vs 26 in the reference lake; thesis p. 17, PDF p. 31), aged from transverse sections of lapillus otoliths read by two readers (p. 10–11, PDF pp. 24–25), spawning-run fish trapped in 2014.

notes: STAND-IN: Begley, M. A. 2016. Understanding the impact of commercial harvest on White Suckers (Catostomus commersonii) in Maine. M.S. thesis, University of Maine (Electronic Theses and Dissertations 2553; title page says 'By Meg Begley', December 2016; co-advisors Zydlewski and Coghlan). Its Chapter 1 is the work published as the 2017 article; recommend citing the thesis (with the Wayback URL) for the age-26 and twofold-mortality statements until the article is read. Lakes are anonymised in the thesis (Harvested-A…C, Reference-A…C). Other thesis values: maximum ages harvested vs reference 9 vs 15, 16 vs 26, 12 vs 22; the thesis's population model used M = 0.97 at age 1 and 0.25 from age 2 (Chapter 2, PDF p. 55), the values Table 3.5-3 credits to Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2018; fecundity in the model ranged 3,910–26,060 eggs (PDF p. 51).
